chapters.title: Titus 1
body: Paul leaves Titus with a specific task — appointing qualified elders across Crete's cities — and the qualifications again center on character rather than status: blameless, self-controlled, hospitable, holding firmly to sound teaching. He pairs this with a blunt warning about false teachers already causing real damage there, quoting a local saying about Cretans being generally unreliable, and insisting the warning applies precisely because it's true, not as an insult for its own sake.

Titus didn't get a tidy, easy assignment; he got a real, specific mess to help organize with real standards rather than vague ones. If the particular mess in front of you right now feels discouraging precisely because it's so ordinary and unglamorous, this chapter's whole premise is that it was still worth doing carefully.

chapters.title: Titus 2
body: Paul asks different groups within the church — older men and women, younger men and women, even servants — to live in ways that make the gospel look credible rather than embarrassing to outsiders, grounding every instruction in grace rather than mere rule-following: "the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men," teaching believers to live well now while looking forward to what's still coming.

These instructions aren't primarily about appearances for their own sake; they're about whether a life actually matches what it claims to believe closely enough for someone watching to find it credible. Whoever is currently watching your own ordinary conduct — not your stated beliefs, but how you actually live — is the test this chapter is quietly describing.

chapters.title: Titus 3
body: Paul closes with instructions toward being good, submissive citizens, avoiding foolish and divisive controversies — and then grounds the whole letter in one clarifying reminder: "not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us." Good works matter deeply to Paul throughout this letter, but they're the result of mercy already given, never the price paid to earn it.

It's easy to quietly slide good behavior back into something you're performing to stay acceptable, even after genuinely believing grace started things off. This chapter's closing reminder is written for exactly that drift — the order was mercy first, and everything else follows from there, not the other way around.
